notes.front: What is a Log Analytics workspace?
notes.back: A data store that holds the tables into which Azure Monitor Logs collects data; it is the primary Azure Monitor Logs resource.
notes.explanation: You can collect, manage and use many types of log data in one workspace without moving data or managing other storage.
notes.example: Like a single warehouse with separate shelves (tables) for each kind of record, where every team goes to look things up.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Monitor Logs overview”, “Log Analytics workspace” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A Log Analytics workspace is a data store that holds tables into which you collect data.

notes.front: What does monitoring virtual machines in Azure Monitor cover?
notes.back: Monitoring the health, performance and availability of Azure VMs and scale sets, using host signals plus optional guest metrics and logs.
notes.explanation: Together this data helps you detect service issues, understand resource pressure and troubleshoot workloads.
notes.example: Like checking a car both from the outside (speed, fuel use) and by plugging into its engine computer for detailed fault codes.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Monitor virtual machines in Azure” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Monitor provides the tools to monitor the health, performance, and availability of Azure virtual machines and virtual machine scale sets. It combines host-level signals that Azure collects automatically with optional metrics and logs from the guest operating system.

notes.front: What is Kubernetes monitoring in Azure Monitor?
notes.back: A set of Azure Monitor services that together monitor the health and performance of each layer of a Kubernetes environment and its applications.
notes.explanation: It covers clusters in Azure Kubernetes Service or other clouds.
notes.example: Like a hospital monitoring a patient with a heart monitor, blood tests and a doctor’s round, each watching a different layer of health.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Kubernetes monitoring in Azure Monitor” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure provides a complete set of services based on Azure Monitor for monitoring the health and performance of different layers of your Kubernetes infrastructure and the applications that depend on it.

notes.front: How do you retrieve data from a Log Analytics workspace?
notes.back: With a Kusto Query Language (KQL) query, a read-only request that processes data and returns results.
notes.explanation: KQL can analyse millions of records quickly.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Monitor Logs overview”, “Kusto Query Language (KQL) and Log Analytics” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You retrieve data from a Log Analytics workspace by using a Kusto Query Language (KQL) query. KQL is a read-only request that processes data and returns results.

notes.front: What are two things you can manage per table or per workspace in a Log Analytics workspace?
notes.back: Any two of: table plans, retention for each table, access to the workspace and to specific tables, summary rules.
notes.explanation: These let one workspace serve the needs of different personas.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Monitor Logs overview”, “Log Analytics workspace” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: - Define table plans based on your data consumption and cost management needs. - Manage low-cost long-term retention and analytics retention for each table. - Manage access to the workspace and to specific tables.

notes.front: A DevOps team must keep verbose audit logs cheaply for years and also keep live performance data for alerting. What does Microsoft suggest?
notes.choices:
A) A separate workspace for every data type
B) One Log Analytics workspace, with a suitable table plan for each kind of data
C) Azure Monitor Metrics for both
D) Export everything to a storage account and query nothing
notes.back: B) One Log Analytics workspace, with a suitable table plan for each kind of data
notes.choicesExplained: A is not needed: one workspace can hold any type of log. C stores numeric time-series data, not verbose audit logs. D gives up the querying and alerting the team needs.
notes.explanation: One workspace can store any type of log, and table plans manage cost by how often data is used.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Monitor Logs overview”, “Table plans” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Use one Log Analytics workspace to store any type of log required for any purpose.

notes.front: Which Log Analytics table plan is best for high-value data used for continuous monitoring and real-time detection?
notes.back: The Analytics plan.
notes.explanation: It is the only plan that includes the query price and supports insights.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Monitor Logs overview”, “Table feature comparison” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: | Best for | High-value data used for continuous monitoring, real-time detection, and performance analytics.

notes.front: Which Log Analytics table plan is meant for medium-touch data needed for troubleshooting and incident response?
notes.back: The Basic plan.
notes.explanation: It has reduced ingestion cost compared with Analytics.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Monitor Logs overview”, “Table feature comparison” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Medium-touch data needed for troubleshooting and incident response.

notes.front: Which Log Analytics table plan suits low-touch verbose logs kept for auditing and compliance?
notes.back: The Auxiliary (Lake) plan.
notes.explanation: It has minimal ingestion cost but slower queries.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Monitor Logs overview”, “Table feature comparison” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Low-touch data, such as verbose logs, and data required for auditing and compliance.

notes.front: What does Application Insights work item integration let you do?
notes.back: Create issues, bugs or tasks in GitHub or Azure DevOps directly from Application Insights, with relevant telemetry included.
notes.explanation: Templates embed KQL queries and workbook content in the new work items.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Work item integration” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Work item integration lets you create issues, bugs, or tasks in GitHub or Azure DevOps directly from Application Insights experiences.

notes.front: Application Insights work item templates are Azure Monitor Workbooks saved as the {{c1::`Microsoft.Insights/workbooks`}} resource type.
notes.explanation: So you can author and automate them like any other workbook, including with ARM templates.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Work item integration” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Work item templates are Azure Monitor Workbooks saved as the `Microsoft.Insights/workbooks` resource type. Author and automate these workbooks like any other workbook.

notes.front: Where do you create a work item template in Application Insights?
notes.back: In the Application Insights resource, under Configure > Work Items > Create a new template.
notes.explanation: You then choose the tracking system, name the workbook and give the default repository address.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Work item integration”, “Create and configure a work item template” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Open your Application Insights resource. Under **Configure**, open **Work Items**, and then select **Create a new template**.

notes.front: An engineer can view Application Insights but cannot save a work item template. Which Azure role would let them?
notes.choices:
A) Reader on the subscription
B) Stakeholder access in Azure DevOps
C) Workbook Contributor or Monitoring Contributor
D) Triage on the GitHub repository
notes.back: C) Workbook Contributor or Monitoring Contributor
notes.choicesExplained: A cannot write workbooks. B and D are rights in the tracking system, which govern creating the work item itself, not the template.
notes.explanation: Creating or editing a template needs a role with `Microsoft.Insights/workbooks/write`, such as these two.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Work item integration”, “Permissions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To create or edit a work item template, use an Azure role with `Microsoft.Insights/workbooks/write`, such as **Workbook Contributor** or **Monitoring Contributor**.

notes.front: From which Application Insights view do you create a work item for a specific event, and what is filled in for you?
notes.back: End-to-end transaction details; it prepopulates context such as exception details, operation name and a link back to the transaction.
notes.explanation: The work item is then created in a new browser tab in GitHub or Azure DevOps.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Work item integration”, “Create work items” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Complete the **New Work Item** pane. Application Insights prepopulates contextual data from the selected event, for example exception details, operation name, and a link back to the transaction.

notes.front: What are release annotations in Application Insights?
notes.back: Markers on Application Insights charts for deployments and other significant events.
notes.explanation: They let you correlate changes with performance, failures and usage.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Investigate failures, performance, and transactions with Application Insights”, “Release annotations” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Release annotations mark deployments and other significant events on Application Insights charts, allowing correlation of changes with performance, failures, and usage.

notes.front: An Azure App Service deployment task runs, the app has `APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING` set, but no release annotation appears. What is the likely cause?
notes.choices:
A) The pipeline has more than one stage
B) The app has no deployment slot
C) The Application Insights resource is in a different subscription from the app
D) Annotations only appear in the Metrics pane
notes.back: C) The Application Insights resource is in a different subscription from the app
notes.choicesExplained: A and B are not among the listed conditions. D is wrong: release annotations are not available in the Metrics pane.
notes.explanation: Azure Pipelines creates the annotation only when the Application Insights resource is in the same subscription as the target resource, among other conditions.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Investigate failures, performance, and transactions with Application Insights”, “Automatic annotations with Azure Pipelines” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: * The target resource links to Application Insights through the `APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING` app setting. > * The Application Insights resource is in the same subscription as the target resource.

notes.front: Your deployment uses none of the tasks that annotate automatically. How do you add a release annotation in the pipeline?
notes.back: Add an Azure CLI task in the deployment stage running the PowerShell annotation script inline.
notes.explanation: The same script can create annotations from any process, without Azure DevOps.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Investigate failures, performance, and transactions with Application Insights”, “Configure annotations in a pipeline by using an inline script” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If you don't use the tasks in the previous section, add an inline script in the deployment stage.

notes.front: When does the Query Azure Monitor alerts check on an Azure Pipelines environment succeed?
notes.back: When no alert rules are activated at the time of evaluation.
notes.explanation: It helps ensure no alerts are raised for the application after a deployment.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Define approvals and checks”, “Query Azure Monitor Alerts” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Query Azure Monitor Alerts helps you observe Azure Monitor and ensure no alerts are raised for the application after a deployment. The check succeeds if no alert rules are activated at the time of evaluation.

notes.front: After a canary deployment to the first group of customers, a team wants the next stage to run only if the application raises no Azure Monitor alerts. What should it add to the next stage’s environment?
notes.choices:
A) A Query Azure Monitor alerts check
B) An exclusive lock
C) A branch control check
D) A Business Hours check
notes.back: A) A Query Azure Monitor alerts check
notes.choicesExplained: B stops concurrent runs, it does not look at health. C checks which branch the run comes from. D limits when a stage may run.
notes.explanation: Microsoft describes this check for staged rollouts: application health after deployment decides whether the update goes to the next stage.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Define approvals and checks”, “Query Azure Monitor Alerts” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: After deploying to a stage (set of customers), the application is observed for a period of time. Health of the application after deployment is used to decide whether the update should be made to the next stage or not.

notes.front: What kind of feature is Application Insights, and which framework can you use to instrument applications for it?
notes.back: An application performance monitoring feature of Azure Monitor; you can use OpenTelemetry (OTel), a vendor-neutral framework.
notes.explanation: For supported scenarios, the telemetry collected with OpenTelemetry is analysed in Application Insights.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Introduction to Application Insights - OpenTelemetry observability” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Monitor Application Insights is an application performance monitoring (APM) feature of Azure Monitor. For supported scenarios, you can use OpenTelemetry (OTel), a vendor-neutral observability framework, to instrument your applications and collect telemetry data

notes.front: For most code-based server-side scenarios, Microsoft recommends instrumenting with the {{c1::Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry Distro}}.
notes.explanation: Scenarios where OpenTelemetry is not available are clearly identified.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Introduction to Application Insights - OpenTelemetry observability”, “Getting started” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: For most code-based server-side scenarios, the recommended setup uses the Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry Distro.

notes.front: A team wants page views and user interactions from its single-page web app in Application Insights. What should it add to the browser app?
notes.choices:
A) The Application Insights JavaScript software development kit
B) The Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry Distro
C) The Azure Monitor agent
D) A diagnostic setting
notes.back: A) The Application Insights JavaScript software development kit
notes.choicesExplained: B is the recommended path for server-side code, not browser apps. C collects guest data on VMs. D exports platform logs and metrics, not browser telemetry.
notes.explanation: Browser apps use the Application Insights JavaScript software development kit, not OpenTelemetry.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Introduction to Application Insights - OpenTelemetry observability”, “Set up data collection” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Use this path for browser telemetry such as page views and user interactions. Browser apps use the Application Insights JavaScript SDK, not OpenTelemetry.

notes.front: To collect data from a server-side web app: create an Application Insights resource, get its {{c1::connection string}}, add the Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry Distro, and configure the connection string.
notes.explanation: The same code-based flow applies to apps running on a VM.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Introduction to Application Insights - OpenTelemetry observability”, “Set up data collection” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: 1. Create an Application Insights resource. 1. Get the resource's connection string. 1. Add the Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry Distro to your app. 1. Configure the connection string.

notes.front: In which group of Application Insights experiences is Live metrics, a real-time analytics dashboard?
notes.back: Investigate.
notes.explanation: Investigate tools help diagnose issues and understand runtime behaviour.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Introduction to Application Insights - OpenTelemetry observability”, “Investigate” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Live metrics: A real-time analytics dashboard for insight into application activity and performance.

notes.front: In which group of Application Insights experiences do you find Alerts, Metrics, Diagnostic settings and Workbooks?
notes.choices:
A) Monitoring
B) Usage
C) Investigate
D) Code analysis
notes.back: A) Monitoring
notes.choicesExplained: C holds diagnostic tools such as Live metrics and the Availability view. B is about how users interact with the app. D profiles and debugs code.
notes.explanation: Monitoring tools track application health continuously and set up proactive notifications.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Introduction to Application Insights - OpenTelemetry observability”, “Monitoring” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Use these tools to continuously track your application's health and set up proactive notifications. * Alerts: Monitor a wide range of aspects of your application and trigger various actions.

notes.front: Which group of Application Insights experiences helps you understand how users interact with your application?
notes.back: Usage.
notes.explanation: It includes the Users, sessions, and events tools, among others.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Introduction to Application Insights - OpenTelemetry observability”, “Usage” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Use these tools to understand how users interact with your application. * Users, sessions, and events: Determine when, where, and how users interact with your web app.

notes.front: In which group of Application Insights experiences is the Snapshot debugger, which collects debug snapshots when exceptions occur?
notes.back: Code analysis.
notes.explanation: Code analysis tools profile and debug application code.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Introduction to Application Insights - OpenTelemetry observability”, “Code analysis” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Use these tools to profile and debug your application code.

notes.front: Host metrics versus guest metrics for Azure VMs: what does each show, and how is each collected?
notes.back: Host metrics show overall performance and load, collected automatically at no cost; guest metrics show processes inside the machine and need enhanced monitoring.
notes.explanation: You might use host metrics to find loaded machines, then guest data to drill in.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Monitor virtual machines in Azure”, “Enable enhanced monitoring” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: - **Host metrics** provide visibility into overall performance and load (CPU usage, network traffic, disk I/O). These are collected automatically at no cost. - **Guest metrics** provide detailed insights into applications, components, and processes running inside the machine.

notes.front: What does enabling enhanced monitoring install on a VM?
notes.back: The Azure Monitor agent, which starts collecting a default set of metrics.
notes.explanation: Enhanced monitoring fully lights up the Monitor view for the VM.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Monitor virtual machines in Azure”, “Enable enhanced monitoring” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Enable enhanced monitoring to collect guest data and fully light up the **Monitor** view in the Azure portal. This process installs Azure Monitor agent on the virtual machine and starts collecting a default set of metrics.

notes.front: What does Azure Monitor create for a VM when you enable enhanced monitoring, besides collecting data?
notes.back: A baseline set of recommended alert rules, whose thresholds, severity and notifications you can customise.
notes.explanation: The recommended rules are based on your monitoring configuration.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Monitor virtual machines in Azure”, “Alerts” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you enable enhanced monitoring, Azure Monitor will create a baseline set of recommended alert rules for the VM based on your monitoring configuration.

notes.front: An operations team must switch on monitoring for 400 VMs and keep new VMs covered automatically. Which approach does Microsoft list for this?
notes.choices:
A) Open the Monitor view of each VM in the portal
B) Enable VM monitoring at scale, for example with Azure Policy
C) Rely on host metrics, which need no set-up
D) Add a diagnostic setting to the subscription only
notes.back: B) Enable VM monitoring at scale, for example with Azure Policy
notes.choicesExplained: A works one VM at a time. C gives no guest data. D sends platform logs somewhere but does not enable VM guest monitoring.
notes.explanation: Monitoring can be enabled at scale with Azure CLI, PowerShell, Azure Policy, ARM templates, Bicep and other IaC tools.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Monitor virtual machines in Azure”, “Enable at scale” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Enable VM monitoring at scale by using Azure CLI, PowerShell, Azure Policy, ARM templates, Bicep, and other infrastructure as code (IaC) tools.

notes.front: VM activity logs versus guest logs: which needs configuring and costs money?
notes.back: Guest logs: you configure them with data collection rules, and ingestion and storage charges apply. Activity logs are automatic and free.
notes.explanation: Activity logs record operations on the VM; guest logs come from the operating system and applications inside it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Monitor virtual machines in Azure”, “Guest logs” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Unlike activity logs, you must configure guest logs before Azure Monitor can collect them, and ingestion and storage charges apply. Create data collection rules to define which logs to collect and where to send them.

notes.front: At which Kubernetes monitoring layer do Network Watcher, Traffic analytics and Network insights work?
notes.back: The network level.
notes.explanation: They monitor the virtual network components that carry traffic to and from the cluster.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Kubernetes monitoring in Azure Monitor”, “Network level” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Virtual network components supporting traffic to and from the Kubernetes cluster are monitored with the following services.

notes.front: At which Kubernetes monitoring layer are deployments, the control plane and node pools, watched by managed Prometheus and container log collection?
notes.back: The container levels.
notes.explanation: They include Kubernetes objects, control plane components and scale sets abstracted as nodes.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Kubernetes monitoring in Azure Monitor”, “Container levels” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The Container levels include Kubernetes objects such as deployments, containers, and replicasets, cluster control plane components including API servers, cloud controller, and kubelet, and virtual machine scale sets abstracted as nodes and node pools.

notes.front: Which service monitors the application level of a Kubernetes environment?
notes.back: Application Insights.
notes.explanation: It gives application performance monitoring, including distributed traces, for apps on the cluster.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Kubernetes monitoring in Azure Monitor”, “Application level” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Application workloads running on your Kubernetes cluster are monitored with the following services.

notes.front: What collects container logs from each node of an AKS cluster, and what does it collect?
notes.back: A containerised version of the Azure Monitor agent; it collects stdout/stderr logs and Kubernetes events.
notes.explanation: You can then analyse the data in the portal or query it with Log Analytics.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Kubernetes monitoring in Azure Monitor”, “Container levels” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure service for AKS and Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes clusters that use a containerized version of the Azure Monitor agent to collect stdout/stderr logs and Kubernetes events from each node in your cluster.

notes.front: A team collects AKS container logs and now wants the cluster’s control plane logs in the same Log Analytics workspace. What should it create?
notes.choices:
A) A diagnostic setting
B) A metric alert
C) A release annotation
D) An action group
notes.back: A) A diagnostic setting
notes.choicesExplained: D defines who is notified by alerts. B evaluates metrics, it does not collect logs. C marks deployments on Application Insights charts.
notes.explanation: Control plane logs are resource logs, collected by creating a diagnostic setting that targets the same workspace.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Kubernetes monitoring in Azure Monitor”, “Container levels” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Control plane logs are implemented as resource logs in Azure Monitor. Create a diagnostic setting to collect these logs in the same Log Analytics workspace as your container logs.

notes.front: Which Azure Monitor service collects Prometheus metrics from Kubernetes clusters, and which query language is it compatible with?
notes.back: Azure Monitor managed service for Prometheus; it is compatible with PromQL.
notes.explanation: Prometheus is the most common tool for metrics from Kubernetes clusters.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Kubernetes monitoring in Azure Monitor”, “Container levels” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Monitor managed service for Prometheus is a fully managed solution that's compatible with the Prometheus query language (PromQL)

notes.front: What must you enable before Storage insights shows data for your storage accounts?
notes.back: Nothing: storage metrics are collected by default.
notes.explanation: There is also no charge to access the feature itself.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Monitoring your storage service with Azure Monitor Storage insights”, “Introduction to Storage insights” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: This feature does not require you to enable or configure anything, the storage metrics from your storage accounts are collected by default.

notes.front: What does the Topology view in Network insights show?
notes.back: Azure virtual networks and connected resources, and their relationships across subscriptions, regions and resource groups.
notes.explanation: You can drill down to one resource, such as a VM, for its traffic and connectivity.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Network insights”, “Topology” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Topology provides an interactive interface to view resources and their relationships in Azure across multiple subscriptions, regions, and resource groups.

notes.front: Who can see a chart you create in GitHub Projects insights?
notes.back: Anyone who can view the project.
notes.explanation: You set the filters, chart type and information shown when you create it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About insights for Projects”
notes.evidence: When you create a chart, you set the filters, chart type, the information displayed, and the chart is available to anyone that can view the project.

notes.front: To create a historical chart in GitHub Projects insights, set the chart’s X-axis to {{c1::"Time"}}.
notes.explanation: Historical charts track changes to the state of project items over time.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About insights for Projects”, “About historical charts”
notes.evidence: To create a historical chart, set your chart's X-axis to "Time."

notes.front: A project lead wants a chart of how much work is completed and how much is left over time, to spot bottlenecks. What should they use in GitHub Projects insights?
notes.choices:
A) The default "Burn up" chart
B) A current chart grouped by assignee
C) The repository’s Actions tab
D) A Dependabot alert list
notes.back: A) The default "Burn up" chart
notes.choicesExplained: B shows the present state, not change over time. C shows workflow runs. D lists vulnerable dependencies.
notes.explanation: The default Burn up chart shows the progress of issues over time, including completed and remaining work.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About insights for Projects”, “About historical charts”
notes.evidence: The default "Burn up" chart allows you to visualize the progress of your issues over time, showing how much work is completed and how much is left to do.

notes.front: A project lead wants a saved chart in GitHub Projects insights that counts only items labelled "bug". What should they do?
notes.choices:
A) Create a new repository for bug issues
B) Add a Dependabot alert rule
C) Change the X-axis to "Time"
D) Click New chart, type a label filter above the chart, then click Save changes
notes.back: D) Click New chart, type a label filter above the chart, then click Save changes
notes.choicesExplained: A is not needed: filters select items within the project. B is unrelated to project charts. C makes a historical chart but does not limit it to bugs.
notes.explanation: Creating a chart means clicking New chart, typing filters above it to change the data, and saving the changes.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating charts”
notes.evidence: 1. Above the chart, type filters to change the data used to build the chart. For more information, see [AUTOTITLE](/issues/planning-and-tracking-with-projects/customizing-views-in-your-project/filtering-projects). 1. To the right of the filter text box, click **Save changes**.

notes.front: In GitHub Projects insights, where do you change a chart’s type and X-axis field?
notes.back: In the Configure panel: the Layout drop-down for type and the X-axis drop-down for the field.
notes.explanation: The same panel offers Group by and Y-axis options.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Configuring charts”
notes.evidence: To change the type of chart, select the **Layout** dropdown and click on the chart type you want to use.

notes.front: With GitHub Actions email or web notifications on, when are you notified about workflow runs?
notes.back: When any workflow run you triggered completes, with its status; you can choose to be notified only of failures.
notes.explanation: Statuses include successful, failed, neutral and cancelled.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Notifications for workflow runs”
notes.evidence: you'll receive a notification when any workflow runs that you've triggered have completed. The notification will include the workflow run's status (including successful, failed, neutral, and canceled runs). You can also choose to receive a notification only when a workflow run has failed.

notes.front: Ana created a scheduled workflow. Ben later changed its cron syntax in the `schedule` event. Who now receives its run notifications?
notes.choices:
A) Ben
B) Ana
C) Every repository administrator
D) Nobody: scheduled workflows send no notifications
notes.back: A) Ben
notes.choicesExplained: B would be right only until someone else edits the cron syntax. C is not how scheduled notifications are routed. D is wrong: they go to one user.
notes.explanation: If a different user updates the cron syntax, later notifications go to that user.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Notifications for workflow runs”
notes.evidence: Notifications for scheduled workflows are sent to the user who initially created the workflow. * If a different user updates the cron syntax, in the `schedule` event in the workflow file, subsequent notifications will be sent to that user instead.

notes.front: Which two Pipelines templates can you use for a team or project notification subscription in Azure DevOps?
notes.back: Run stage waiting for approval, and Run stage waiting for manual validation.
notes.explanation: These are the templates listed for the Pipelines category.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About notifications”, “Team and project-level notifications” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence:
| Pipelines | _Run stage waiting for approval_,
_Run stage waiting for manual validation_ |

notes.front: A team wants an email to the whole team whenever a build fails in its Azure DevOps project. What should the team administrator create?
notes.choices:
A) A personal subscription on each member’s account
B) A GitHub Actions workflow run notification
C) A team notification subscription from the Build fails template
D) A Query Azure Monitor alerts check
notes.back: C) A team notification subscription from the Build fails template
notes.choicesExplained: A works but must be repeated per person. B is a GitHub feature. D is a deployment check, not a notification.
notes.explanation: Team notification subscriptions can use Build templates such as Build completes and Build fails.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About notifications”, “Team and project-level notifications” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: | Build | _Build completes_, _Build fails_,

notes.front: Which Azure Monitor alert type evaluates resource metrics at regular intervals and can use dynamic thresholds?
notes.back: Metric alerts.
notes.explanation: The metrics can be platform, custom, converted log or Application Insights metrics.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Overview of Azure Monitor alerts”, “Types of alerts” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Metric alerts evaluate resource metrics at regular intervals. Metrics can be platform metrics, custom metrics, logs from Azure Monitor converted to metrics, or Application Insights metrics. Metric alerts can also apply multiple conditions and use dynamic thresholds.

notes.front: Which Azure Monitor alert type uses a Log Analytics query to evaluate resource logs at a set frequency?
notes.back: Log search alerts.
notes.explanation: Simple log search alerts are a variant that evaluates each row individually.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Overview of Azure Monitor alerts”, “Types of alerts” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Log search alerts allow users to use a Log Analytics query to evaluate resource logs at a predefined frequency.

notes.front: Which Azure Monitor alert type fires when a new matching activity log event occurs, and includes Service Health alerts?
notes.back: Activity log alerts.
notes.explanation: Resource Health and Service Health alerts are activity log alerts.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Overview of Azure Monitor alerts”, “Types of alerts” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Activity log alerts are triggered when a new activity log event occurs that matches defined conditions. Resource Health alerts and Service Health alerts are activity log alerts that report on your service and resource health.

notes.front: Stateful versus stateless Azure Monitor alerts: how often does each fire?
notes.back: Stateless alerts fire every time the condition is met; stateful alerts fire once and not again until the condition is resolved.
notes.explanation: All activity log alerts are stateless.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Overview of Azure Monitor alerts”, “Alerts and state” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: - Stateless alerts fire each time the condition is met, even if fired previously. - Stateful alerts fire when the rule conditions are met, and will not fire again or trigger any more actions until the conditions are resolved.
